title: Rights Came, and Jahiliyyah Came Back • When a Human Being Is Merchandise • Those Who Had No Name Received One • The Chain Has Been Opened, Yet • The One With No One Behind Him • The Day Allah Stood Behind the Weak • Even Today, the One With No One Behind Him • The Price of a She-Camel • Two Tribes, One Row

blocks.0: Rights Came, and Jahiliyyah Came Back
blocks.1: Now let us look at today. Today’s girl has everything that the girl of fourteen hundred years ago did not have. She has the right to give her opinion. No one can marry her off without telling her. She goes to school. She goes to college. She goes to university. She steps outside the home. She works. She keeps the money she earns in her own hands. The girl of the desert could not have imagined a single one of these. Now the question is, what are we doing with these rights?
blocks.2: A girl has come from the village to the city. Her father sold land. Her mother raises her hands in supplication after every prayer. The whole village knows that their girl studies at the university. The first few months went well. Then she met someone. First talk about class. Then talk on the phone. Then talking late into the night. The girl thought, this is nothing at all. Then sitting together. Eating together. Going about together. The girl thought, this too is nothing at all. In this way, at every step she convinced herself, this much is nothing at all. And every step carried her one step closer to the next. Satan never invites to a great sin on the very first day. He only asks you to take one small step. Then the day she had given everything, the boy said, we never said we would marry.
blocks.3: In the village the father still says proudly, my daughter studies at the university. And the mother still raises her hands after prayer. Another house. The girl has been married. She has a child. She has a husband. She goes to the office. There is a colleague there. First talk about work. Then talk that is not about work. She realises that her husband has never spoken to her like this. Her husband has been carrying the household for ten years. He leaves at dawn, returns at night. His body is tired, there is no smile on his face. And this man says every morning, you look very beautiful today. The crack begins with just this much. Then one day the household breaks apart. The child asks, where is Mummy? And there is no answer to the question.
blocks.4: In another house the breaking comes in another way. The woman earns. Sometimes more than her husband. And that money slowly becomes a weapon. At every turn she says, am I dependent on you? She says, if I were not here, would this household run? Her husband falls silent. Then small insults keep piling up. One day they pile up so high that the house is no longer a home. Islam gave woman ownership of wealth, yes. But not so that it might be made a tool for breaking the household.
blocks.5: Now step out of the house and stand on the road. At the corner a billboard. Fifty feet high. On it a picture of a girl. But the advertisement is not for her. The advertisement is for a soap. Or a mobile phone. Or steel rods. What relation does the girl have to steel rods? None. She has been placed there because sales go up when people look. That is, she herself is not the product. She is an instrument for selling the product. Such is the side of the screen. Cinema, drama, song. There a girl is acting. But the next day people do not discuss her acting. They discuss something else. And she knows it. She knows that her real job is not acting. And after that there is the trade whose name one is ashamed even to say. There is no pretence left there. There the girl is directly a commodity.
blocks.6: She can be seen. Bought. Sold. Then thrown away. And that girl too has a mother. No one remembers that. This very society shouts the slogan, woman is no commodity. And in this very society’s market the most profitable commodity is the woman’s body. One thing on the tongue. Another in the account book.
blocks.7: Now let me say the hardest thing. Where does the end of this road finally lead? Someone is used and thrown away. Someone falls into the trap of blackmail. Someone’s picture ends up in a place from where it will never be erased. And some end up in a place where their will has no value at all. Today’s boys must first look at themselves. The boy who ruins a girl’s life in the name of love, what answer will he give tomorrow on the plain of Resurrection? He too is somebody’s brother. He too will one day be somebody’s father.
blocks.8: The calculation is this. The girl of that day had no rights. So she was used. Today’s girl has rights. Yet she is being used. The difference is only one. On that day she was taken by force. Today she is persuaded. On that day the chain was put on the hand. Today the chain is put on the mind. And a chain put on the mind, people do not even recognise as a chain. She thinks, I am free.
blocks.9: Jahiliyyah has returned. But not with its old face. No one buries a girl in the ground any more. No one hangs flags on doors any more. Today’s Jahiliyyah comes in the name of freedom. It comes in the name of rights. It comes in the name of modernity. On that day people knew, this is darkness. Today people do not even know that this is darkness. And this is exactly what has made today’s Jahiliyyah harder than that day’s. The patient who knows he is ill at least looks for medicine. And the one who thinks he is well! The right was given by Allah. The Prophet {{1}} gave it with his own hands. But along with that right he had also given a limit. We took the right. We left the limit behind.
blocks.10: When a Human Being Is Merchandise
blocks.11: The fair of ‘Ukaz. Morning. In one corner a few people have been made to stand in a row. A buyer came and stood. He took one man’s face and made him open his mouth. He looked at the teeth. Then he pressed the muscles of his arm. Then he told him to walk a few steps. Exactly what people do when buying a horse. Then the bargaining began. The man is standing. His own price is being fixed in front of him. And he cannot say a single word. Because merchandise does not have the right to speak. One thing these people did not have. Lineage. In Arabia a person’s identity was in his father’s name; so-and-so, son of so-and-so. A slave was called by his owner’s name. So-and-so’s slave. That is, he is no one’s son. He is someone’s property.
blocks.12: And not everyone who stood in this market had been a slave from birth. The story is this. In a tribe towards Syria there was a boy. His father’s name was Harithah. His mother’s name was Su‘da. One day the mother took the boy to visit her parents’ home. On the way bandits fell upon them. They carried the boy off. Then they brought him to the market of ‘Ukaz and sold him. The price rose to four hundred dirhams. The boy was then eight or nine years old. In the morning he was the child of a free man. By evening he had become someone’s merchandise. And his father’s name was wiped from his name.
blocks.13: The father’s side was this. Harithah set out to search for his son. From one tribe to another. From one fair to another. No one could tell him. He composed poetry for his son, and kept reciting that poetry along the roads. I weep when the dove coos. I do not know whether he is alive or not. I only know that I keep searching. Year after year. Meanwhile the boy did not know that his father was searching for him. And the father did not know where the boy was. Two people, under the same sky. And in between, the receipt of a market.
blocks.14: And what was the worth of a slave’s life anyway? If the owner wished, he could kill him. No one would ask. Because to ask, one needs a tribe. And a slave has no tribe. When a free man was killed, a forty-year war would break out. And when a slave was killed! A piece of merchandise was spoiled, that was all.
blocks.15: Those Who Had No Name Received One
blocks.16: Do you remember that stolen boy? The one who bought him presented him as a gift to Khadijah (RA). And Khadijah gave him to her husband. Prophethood had not yet come. Some days later, in the Hajj season, a few men of the boy’s tribe came to Makkah and saw him. The news reached the father. Harithah rushed over. With him the ransom money. He said, take whatever sum is needed; only let my boy go. Muhammad {{1}} said, no money is needed. Call the boy. Whomever he chooses, with him he will go. The father was glad. Would a son stay away from his father? The boy was called. He said, I will not leave this man for anywhere. The father was stunned. He said, you are choosing slavery over freedom! The boy said, I have received from this man something I have received from no one.
blocks.17: Then Muhammad {{1}} took his hand, went and stood at the Hatim. Then he called the Quraysh and said, be witnesses; from today Zayd is free, and he is my son. Later, in Surah al-Ahzab, Allah abolished the custom of calling an adopted son by one’s own name; from then on he was again known by his own father’s name, Zayd ibn Harithah.{{2}}
blocks.19: That day a boy sold in the market of Makkah recovered a lineage. Even before prophethood. After prophethood, he first changed the language of calling. He said, do not call them ‘my slave’, ‘my slave-girl’. Say, my boy, my girl.{{1}}
blocks.20: Then he said what no one in that age had even imagined. He said, they are your brothers. So whatever you eat, feed them the same. Whatever you wear, clothe them in the same. And do not burden them with work beyond their ability.{{1}}
blocks.21: The saying did not stop there. Whatever you eat, feed them the same. Rice from the same pot. The same cloth. Then he opened the doors of freeing slaves one after another. Broke an oath! Free a slave. Broke a fast! Free a slave. Killed someone by mistake! Free a slave. And when the Qur’an described the difficult path, the very first thing it named was this too.
blocks.23: And what will make you know what the steep pass is? It is the freeing of a neck.{{1}}
blocks.24: Prayer or fasting was not set as the expiation for sins. What was set was the loosening of a person’s chain. Zayd (RA) later became a commander. And the last army that the Prophet {{1}} sent before his death, he made Zayd’s son Usamah its commander. Usamah was then about eighteen or twenty. And in that army were the senior Companions among the Muhajirun and the Ansar.{{2}}
blocks.25: Some people raised talk. The Prophet {{1}} stood on the pulpit and said, you are talking about his command! Before this you also raised talk about his father’s command. And by Allah, he was fit for command. The calculation is this. A boy sold at four hundred dirhams in the market of ‘Ukaz. His son, commander of the entire Muslim army. And standing under him are the most noble men of the Quraysh.
blocks.26: The Chain Has Been Opened, Yet
blocks.27: Today there is no slavery. Not in law. Not on paper. But inside our own homes it is like this. The person who comes in the morning and mops the house, cooks, minds the children. Where does she sit to eat at noon? At the same table as you? Or on the kitchen floor? The curry you eat, does she eat that? Or is something separate kept aside for her? Is her plate separate? The Prophet {{1}} said, whatever you eat, feed them the same. A saying from fourteen hundred years ago. And today!
blocks.28: In Jahili Arabia a person’s standing was decided by his lineage. Today it is decided by his money. In those days one who had no tribe was nobody. Today one who has no money is nobody. The measure has not changed. Only its name has. And he came and broke this very measure. The one who declared a sold boy to be his own son is our Prophet. And we are his Ummah. Tonight one thing can be done. Call the person who works in the house, sit her beside you and eat together. You will see that a Sunnah of the Prophet {{1}} has returned to your home.
blocks.29: The One With No One Behind Him
blocks.30: A house in Makkah. The man has died. He has left a son and some camels. The boy is seven. By the rule, the uncle is the guardian. The camels are now in the uncle’s pen. In the first year the uncle took one of his nephew’s fat camels, and tied a thin camel of his own in its place. The number is right, after all. The second year, another. The third year, another. No one says anything. Because there is no such thing as an account book. There is no such thing as a witness. What there is, is the uncle’s word.{{1}}
blocks.31: The boy grew up. One day he went and stood before him. He said, uncle, now hand over my father’s property. The uncle raised his face and looked. Then he said, what property! Who fed you all these years? The boy stood silent. Where would he go? Justice is held in the gathering of the tribe’s elders. And those who sit in that gathering are all this very uncle’s own people. To whom would he complain? When the one in whose hand is justice is himself the opposing party; then the wronged has nowhere else to go.
blocks.32: Now another scene. A desert road. A lone traveller. He has a few camels, some goods. On the road a few men came and surrounded him. He cried out. There were tents in the distance. There were people. No one came. Why did no one come? Because before that a question is asked. Which tribe is the man from? If the tribe is large, saving him today will be useful tomorrow. If the tribe is small, saving him today will multiply enemies tomorrow. And if he has no tribe at all! Then the calculation is easy; it is better not to go.
blocks.33: Here the real face of Arabia’s system of justice comes out. It is not that they had no justice. They did. But it was not justice of law; it was justice of fear. The more swords behind you, the greater your right. If no one is behind you, you have no right. There is an example of how far it went. In Madinah there were two Jewish tribes; Banu al-Nadir and Banu Qurayzah. The Nadir were strong. The Qurayzah weak. If anyone of the Qurayzah killed anyone of the Nadir, he had to pay with his life. And if anyone of the Nadir killed anyone of the Qurayzah! He did not have to give his life. The matter was settled with a hundred wasq of dates.{{1}}
blocks.34: The same crime. Two kinds of justice. Because one had people behind him, the other did not. Among the Arab tribes too, the same disease. Some tribes would say, two of yours for one of ours. A slave of yours will not do in place of a free man of ours. A woman of yours will not do in place of a man of ours.{{1}}
blocks.35: That is, even the price of a human life was not the same. The price was fixed by looking at lineage. And on the very bottom floor it was like this. A labourer worked all day. In the evening he stood waiting for his wages. The owner said, come tomorrow. The next day he came. The owner said, come later. He does not come any more. Because he knows that asking will do nothing; rather, the job will also be lost. His labour was taken from him, and the price was not paid. This incident was entered in no register. Because in the register of Jahiliyyah the name of the weak is not written.
blocks.36: The Day Allah Stood Behind the Weak
blocks.37: The first light fell on this darkness through a verse of the Qur’an. Allah caught the calculation of that uncle—
blocks.39: And give the orphans their property. And do not exchange the bad for the good. And do not consume their property along with your own property. Indeed, that is a great sin.{{1}}
blocks.40: How subtle it is! Allah did not only say, do not steal the orphan’s property. He said, do not exchange the bad for the good. That is, the trick of keeping the number right while changing the quality was caught too. The wrong that had no name at all was given a name. Then came that verse, which makes the body tremble to hear—
blocks.42: Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly are only filling their bellies with fire. And soon they will enter a blazing fire.{{1}}
blocks.43: The uncle who thought no one was watching was told: it is being watched. And the account will not end in this world. After this the Qur’an pointed a finger at the whole society. In Surah al-Fajr Allah, as it were, counted the faults off one by one. You do not honour the orphan. You do not urge one another to feed the poor. You devour inheritance greedily. And you love wealth blindly.{{1}}
blocks.44: A picture of a whole society in four sentences. But the Qur’an did not stop with a rebuke. It took the weak one’s hand. And the work of taking that hand was given to one who had himself been an orphan. Allah reminded him—
blocks.46: So as for the orphan, do not oppress him. And as for the one who asks, do not scold him.{{1}}
blocks.47: The one who never saw his own father’s face, by his hand the rights of the orphan were written. And the honour he declared for the guardian of an orphan was something the Arabs had not even imagined. He said, I and the one who cares for an orphan will be in Paradise like this.{{1}}
blocks.48: The child who was not even allowed to stand in the tribe’s gathering, caring for him became the way to be beside the Prophet {{1}}. After this he laid his hand on the hardest place. The price of a life. Coming to Madinah he abolished that discrimination between al-Nadir and Qurayzah. Then he stated the rule; the blood of Muslims is equal. And what he joined to it was even more astonishing. He said, the protection granted by Muslims is one; even the humblest of them, if he grants protection to anyone, all must honour it.{{2}}
blocks.49: In a society where the weak one’s word had no weight, the word of the weakest person bound the whole state. On the day of the conquest of Makkah, Umm Hani (RA) gave refuge to two polytheists. ‘Ali (RA) did not want to let them go. The Prophet {{1}} said, whom you have sheltered, we too have sheltered.{{2}}
blocks.50: One woman’s single word. And above it no one else’s word ran. Then he went and stood beside that labourer. He said, Allah has said, on the Day of Resurrection I will be the adversary of three. One who makes a pledge in My name and then breaks it. One who sells a free person and eats his price. And one who hires a labourer, takes the whole work from him, yet does not pay his wages.{{1}}
blocks.51: The word is important here. Allah did not say, I will punish him. He said, I will be his adversary. That is, on one side of the case he, and on the other side Allah Himself. The labourer who had no one to stand for him, for him the Lord of the Throne stood. And he fixed the time for paying wages too. He said, pay him his wages before his sweat dries.{{1}}
blocks.52: Not tomorrow. Not later. Before the sweat dries. And lastly he made oppression itself known in such a way that after knowing it, a mistake should not be possible. He said, oppression will come as darkness on the Day of Resurrection.{{1}}
blocks.53: And the last words he said when sending Mu‘adh (RA) to Yemen are worth remembering. He said, beware the supplication of the oppressed; for there is no veil between it and Allah.{{1}}
blocks.54: The oppressed may not be able to go to anyone. But one door of his is always open. And before that door there is no guard.
blocks.55: Even Today, the One With No One Behind Him
blocks.56: Today in our society there is no tribe. There is no gathering of elders either. There are courts. There are laws. There is paper. Even so, the calculation is this. In a house the father died. He left a son, and some land. The boy is seven. The uncles said, the boy is small; we will look after the land. The statement is not false either. They truly did look after it. For twenty years.
blocks.57: The boy grew up and one day went and stood before him. The uncle raised his face and looked. Then he said, what land! Who fed you all these years? Fourteen hundred years have passed. The sentence has not changed in the least. He went to court. The law is on his side. The papers are on his side. Yet the years kept rolling. One date, then another date. The lawyer’s fees. Travel costs. The loss of working days. And on the other side the uncle has time, has money, has people. After ten years the boy counted and saw that in running the case more than the price of the land had gone. Then he stopped. Not defeated. Exhausted.
blocks.58: Now the real point. In Jahili Arabia, to get justice you needed swords behind you. Today, to get justice you need money behind you, time, people you know. For one who has not even one of these three, the law remains on paper. The condition has not changed. Only the name of the condition has. And do you remember that labourer? He is standing even today. The work is finished. Now, the money. The owner said, come next week. He came. He was told, sir is not in. The third time he did not come. Because the fare for going and coming is itself a third of what he is owed.
blocks.59: The man never came back. The owner thought, thank goodness. He does not know that the complaint has gone up. And who will be his adversary in the court of that complaint, the Prophet {{1}} said it fourteen hundred years ago. One thing we often forget. Oppression does not mean only beating. Oppression means withholding someone’s due. Oppression means not listening to someone’s word because he is weak. Oppression means delaying giving what is his. And these three things happen in our homes, and no one even calls it oppression.
blocks.60: The one who set a common woman’s grant of refuge above the decision of a whole state is our Prophet. And we are his Ummah. So take two works from today’s lesson. One, if anyone’s due is held back in your hand, give it today. However small. Two, if among your relatives some orphan’s right is held back in someone’s hand, at least raise the matter. Speaking a word for the oppressed is also a work. Because standing behind the one who has no one behind him is the greatest Sunnah.
blocks.62: A pasture. On the grass a she-camel is grazing. Her name is Sarab. She belongs to an old woman named al-Basus. Grazing, she mistakenly strayed into the neighbouring tribe’s boundary. Far off stood the leader of that tribe, Kulayb. He raised his bow. The arrow went and pierced the she-camel’s udder. Milk flowed with blood onto the ground. The she-camel limped back to the front of the tent. Al-Basus came out and saw. Then she cried out— my humiliation! my humiliation! That one cry was enough. That very day a young man of her tribe went and killed Kulayb. Then Kulayb’s tribe took revenge. Then revenge again. Then again.
blocks.63: That war lasted forty years. What does forty years mean? Those who had started the war grew old and died. Their sons fought. When the sons died, the grandsons fought. The child born in the first year of the war grew up and fought in the war, married, and had a son. That son too grew up and went to the very same war. Toward the end many could no longer even remember what it had started over. A she-camel’s udder. Its price was paid with thousands upon thousands of lives of two tribes.
blocks.64: Another war was called Dahis and Ghabra’. The names of two horses. A wager on a horse race had been made between two tribes. During the race one side put men on the road and blocked the other side’s horse. From this, quarrelling. Then scuffling. Then blood. That blood stopped after several decades.{{1}}
blocks.65: The causes together are like this. A she-camel crossed a boundary. Someone cheated in a horse race. Someone said a bitter word about someone’s tribe. Someone’s camel drank from someone’s well. This much was enough. To kill people they needed no great cause. And more terrible than this was the second side. They did not forget this blood. The wars did not run continuously. In between, years upon years passed in silence. But the enmity did not die. It was stored up inside the home. The tent at night. By the fire, a five-year-old boy in his father’s lap. The first lesson, genealogy. The second lesson, the account of blood. Banu so-and-so killed three of ours. Your grandfather’s blood has still not been avenged. The child is reciting it all in a lisping voice. No one has told him where he came from. No one has told him where he will go. No one has taught him the name of Allah.
blocks.66: But he knows, Banu so-and-so are our enemies. The revenge for one blood would be stored up for three or four generations. No one forgot. No one forgave either. The reason lay within their system. A tribe that could not take revenge, the poets wrote satirical verse about them. That verse spread from mouth to mouth. And lived on, generation after generation. To forgive meant lasting disgrace. So they had no way except to take revenge. With one killing was born the next killing. And with it the one after. The chain stopped nowhere.
blocks.68: In Madinah there were two tribes. Aws and Khazraj. Their enmity was a hundred and twenty years old.{{1}}
blocks.69: The last war was called Bu‘ath. The blood of that war had not yet dried. The Prophet {{1}} came to Madinah. Within a few years, the people of those two tribes were standing in one row to pray. Standing beside the man who had killed his father. Shoulder to shoulder. Allah preserved that event in the Qur’an.
blocks.71: And remember the favour of Allah upon you, when you were enemies of one another; then He joined your hearts, and by His grace you became brothers.{{1}}
blocks.72: Allah did not say, I stopped their war. He said, I put affection in the hearts. Stopping a war is easy. For that a strong ruler is enough. But wiping out a hundred and twenty years of hatred! That is not a ruler’s work. Then came the day of the Farewell Hajj. The plain of ‘Arafah. Before him more than a hundred thousand people. Almost every one of these people had an account of blood stored up at home. Someone’s father had been killed. Someone’s brother. Someone’s son. He declared, all blood-vengeance of Jahiliyyah is cancelled from today. All. The account of four generations of a whole people was wiped out in one sentence. But he did not stop here. He said, and the first blood I forgive is that of my own clan. The blood of the infant son of Rabi‘ah ibn al-Harith.{{1}}
blocks.73: He did not ask others to forgive. He began with the blood of his own house. After this no one has anything left to say. And the greatest change came in ‘asabiyyah. Above the tribe, which had been the only identity, he set taqwa. In that same sermon he said— there is no superiority of an Arab over a non-Arab. Nor of a non-Arab over an Arab. Nor of the white over the black. Nor of the black over the white. Superiority is only in taqwa. And the Qur’an stated the reason.
blocks.75: O mankind! I created you from one male and one female; and I made you into different nations and tribes, so that you may know one another. Indeed, the most honoured among you in the sight of Allah is the one who has the most taqwa.{{1}}
blocks.76: Tribes will remain. But a tribe is only a name of identity. Not a measure of honour. So beside the son of a chief of Makkah stood the Abyssinian slave Bilal. And on the day the time came to climb the roof of the Ka‘bah and call the adhan, he called Bilal. Those on whose chests a stone had once been laid, their voice that day flowed over the whole of Makkah.

quiz.q: How did the lesson view informing a girl of her marriage without taking her consent?
o: Her silence is full consent
Her silence is not permission, but fear
Her silence is an expression of shyness
Her silence is part of an age-old custom
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ said that silence is permission; but that silence was free, not out of fear.

quiz.q: What is the lesson’s assessment of using a woman’s picture in an advertisement for steel rods?
o: She is a partner of the advertising firm
She herself is a commodity being sold
She is not the commodity, but an instrument for selling the commodity
She is an independent bearer of publicity
quiz.e: She has no relation to the rods; she is placed there because sales go up when people look.

quiz.q: What is the meaning of ‘On that day the chain was put on the hand, today it is put on the mind’?
o: There are no chains anywhere now
The prisoner understands his own imprisonment
The free person thinks himself imprisoned
The prisoner learns to think himself free
quiz.e: A chain put on the mind, people do not even recognise as a chain; she thinks, I am free.

quiz.q: How did Zayd ibn Harithah (RA) fall into slavery?
o: Sold in place of his father’s debt
Captured as a prisoner in a tribal war
Falling into the hands of bandits on the road with his mother
By birth, in the house of a slave mother
quiz.e: Kidnapped at the age of eight or nine, he was sold in the market of ‘Ukaz for four hundred dirhams.

quiz.q: What was revealed by the custom of calling a slave by his owner’s name instead of his father’s name?
o: He is an honoured member of the tribe
He is no one’s son, he is someone’s property
He is an adopted child of the owner’s house
He is a person held captive temporarily
quiz.e: In Arabia identity was in the father’s name; a slave was called by his owner’s name.

quiz.q: Which instruction about slaves came in the hadith narrated by Abu Dharr (RA)?
o: Double their wages right now
Make a separate arrangement for their lodging
Reduce their working hours
Feed them what you eat, clothe them in what you wear
quiz.e: Hadith 30 of Sahih al-Bukhari; he said, they are your brothers.

quiz.q: In describing the ‘steep pass’ in Surah al-Balad, which deed came first?
o: Freeing a neck
Feeding an orphan on a day of hunger
Giving shelter to a close-kin orphan
Counselling one another to patience
quiz.e: Not prayer or fasting even as expiation for sins; what was set was the loosening of a person’s chain.

quiz.q: What is the significance of setting the freeing of a slave, instead of prayer or fasting, as expiation for sins?
o: To make the rule of expiation easier, as is generally held
To show the importance of worship as less
To give priority to a person’s freedom
To bring down the wealth in the hands of the rich
quiz.e: As the remedy for sin, what was set was the loosening of a person’s chain.

quiz.q: What action is given at the end of the lesson regarding the person who works in the home?
o: To sit her beside you and eat together
To raise her salary
To reduce her working hours
To give her a separate room
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ said, whatever you eat, feed them the same; rice from the same pot, the same cloth.

quiz.q: ‘Today one who has no money is nobody’: this is a new face of which Jahili principle?
o: Having a sword means being a hero
No tribe means he is nobody
Having a poet means the tribe is strong
A great lineage means he is honoured
quiz.e: In those days standing was decided by lineage; today it is decided by money.

quiz.q: The discrimination in blood-price between Banu al-Nadir and Banu Qurayzah was
o: The blood-price of both tribes was equal
If one of the Nadir killed, it was settled with a hundred wasq of dates
If one of the Qurayzah killed, only a fine had to be paid
Both tribes left the matter to a judge; this is how it is generally held
quiz.e: Hadith 4494 of Sunan Abi Dawud; if one of the Qurayzah killed, he had to pay with his life.

quiz.q: What was the real condition for getting justice in Jahili Arabia, according to the lesson?
o: Being close to the tribal chief; this is how it is generally held
Being able to present witnesses and proof
How many swords were behind you decided the size of your right
Being willing to take an oath before the Ka‘bah
quiz.e: They had justice, but not the justice of law; the justice of fear.

quiz.q: What did Allah say in the hadith qudsi about the labourer’s wages?
o: I will give him severe punishment
I will not accept his deeds
On the Day of Resurrection I will be his adversary
I will constrict his provision; this is how it is generally held
quiz.e: Hadith 2270 of Sahih al-Bukhari; among the three is the one who hires a labourer, takes the whole work, and does not pay the wages.

quiz.q: What is the subtlety of saying ‘do not exchange the bad for the good’ in Surah al-Nisa’, verse 2?
o: The orphan’s property must not be touched at all; this is how it is generally held
The trick of keeping the number right while changing the quality was caught too
The orphan’s property may be divided
The guardian has no remuneration
quiz.e: The wrong that had no name at all was given a name.

quiz.q: How does the lesson show the significance of ‘the protection granted by Muslims is one’?
o: Only the head of state can grant protection
Protection must be granted with the tribal chief’s permission; this is how it is generally held
Consultation is necessary before granting protection
The word of the weakest person bound the whole state
quiz.e: On the day of the conquest of Makkah the Prophet ﷺ upheld the refuge given by Umm Hani’ (RA).

quiz.q: What is the Prophet’s ﷺ warning to Mu‘adh (RA) regarding the supplication of the oppressed?
o: There is no veil between it and Allah
His supplication is accepted within three days
His supplication is accepted only at night
By his supplication the wealth of the oppressor is destroyed
quiz.e: Hadith 1496 of Sahih al-Bukhari; even if the oppressed cannot go to anyone, one door of his is always open.

quiz.q: On withholding someone’s due, the definition of oppression this lesson gives is
o: Oppression means only physical harm
Withholding a due, not listening to a word, and delaying giving are oppression too
Oppression is possible only for the powerful
It is oppression only if proved in court
quiz.e: And these three things happen in our homes, yet no one even calls it oppression.

quiz.q: What is the significance of ‘He put affection in the hearts’ in Surah Al ‘Imran?
o: The natural result of weariness from a long war
The result of a strong ruler’s firm hand
The result of a written agreement between the two sides
Not outside pressure, but inner change
quiz.e: To stop a war a strong ruler is enough; but wiping out a hundred and twenty years of hatred is not.

quiz.q: What is the significance of beginning with his own clan both in the blood-vengeance and in the usury at the Farewell Hajj?
o: Reform begins from one’s own home
His own clan’s account was the greatest
Because others’ accounts would be dealt with later
Because the people of the clan had raised objections
quiz.e: He did not ask others to forgive; he began with the blood of his own house and the usury of his own uncle.
